thread.title: Will The Bull Market Survive 2018 Intact?

author: Clif Droke
title: Will The Bull Market Survive 2018 Intact?
text:
It has been a tough time to be a bull this fall, and the stock market’s latest action has done nothing to improve this. As we’ll discuss in today’s comments, however, the bulls shouldn’t lose faith and even have some short-term factors in their favor which suggest a correction low will soon be established. Here we’ll examine these factors as I make the case that a year-end rally can still be expected despite the weak internal condition which still prevails.
Wall Street completely forgot its optimism from last week after China’s expressed a willingness to make a trade deal with the U.S. Last Friday’s rally was also based on expectations of an interest rate cut by the Bank of China. This allowed investors to temporarily forget their concerns over the slowing global economy.
On Monday, however, investors' focus had returned to the possibility of a global slowdown as well as uncertainty over the U.S. interest rate outlook. Tech stocks were loss leaders, with Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) leading the rout. Shares of Apple declined nearly 4% after a report was published which said the company would cut production orders on all three iPhones which were launched in September. The company reportedly reduced its production plans by up to one-third of the 70 million units it had asked its suppliers to produce between September and February.
In the wake of this news, the Nasdaq Composite Index lost 3% and closed at its lowest level since May at just above the 7,200 level. The S&P 500 (SPX), meanwhile, gave back its gain from the last two sessions, falling 1.66% and threatening to test its October low. Earlier this month, the SPX had recovered more than half its losses since the October sell-off. The NASDAQ Composite had also retraced a little more than half its losses from October. Since then, however, the major averages have pulled back and are in various stages of the process of testing the October lows. This was what I anticipated would happen as discussed in past reports, and it’s normal behavior for a bull market correction.
At the time of the sell-off in late October, I also mentioned that the decline was mainly the result of Wall Street’s overreaction to rising U.S. interest rates and the emerging markets slowdown. We discussed the fact that most panics are usually completely reversed within 3-4 months of the initial sell-off. If the losses aren’t recovered within a few months, however, it can be assumed that the initial panic selling is part of a much bigger market decline or bear market.
Source: BigCharts
With that in mind, are investors right to worry that we may be on the cusp of another bear market heading into 2019? If you're a regular reader of my commentaries you already know my answer. The weight of evidence from corporate fundamentals, liquidity and currency factors, long-term momentum, and the state of the U.S. economy itself, all argue against a bear market being imminent. Of course that’s cold comfort when the stock market is plumbing the depths of the October decline and threatening to continue to fall even lower. What, then, will serve as the catalyst to reverse the market’s decline? While this remains anyone’s guess, I would argue that what started the correction in the first place, namely the fear generated by spiking bond yields, will dissipate in the coming weeks. This by extension should lift any residual selling pressure from the equity market.
Shown here is the CBOE 10-Year Treasury Note Yield Index (TNX), which illustrates the upward path of bond rates in recent months. It was the acceleration of this rising yield trend in September which served as a catalyst for the October plunge. The rising rate trend encouraged investors to liquidate rate-sensitive stocks and funds, which in turn manifested in a huge increase in the number of 52-week lows on the NYSE. This, more than any other factor, weakened the stock market’s internal structure and made it easy for the bears to take control of the short-term trend.
Source: BigCharts
In the last several days, however, bond yields have begun to pull back as can be seen in the TNX graph above. This is virtually the same pattern we saw during the stock market’s last correction in February-March. After a spike in Treasury yields in January, bond yields drifted lower in March, which allowed the equity market enough time and incentive to bottom out and strengthen. The pullback in Treasury yields in March also allowed the number of NYSE-listed securities making new 52-week lows to shrink, which served to greatly improve the stock market’s internal health. This, more than any other factor, paved the way for the six-month stock market rally which began in April.
The latest decline in Treasury bond yields is definitely a step in the right direction as far as setting the stage for a stock market bottom. The bottom to the October-November correction isn’t in yet, but could be in by the end of this month. I’ll venture that as long as TNX remains subdued and doesn’t rise to a new high from here, the stock market should be able to make the necessary internal improvements by early December and in time for a year-end rally.
Providing anecdotal support for an end to the stock market correction in the next couple of weeks is the recent internal momentum profile for the NYSE. Below is a graph of the 4-week new 52-week highs and lows, which reflects the stock market’s short-term path of least resistance. Even though there are still too many stocks making new 52-week lows versus highs, the rate of change (momentum) of the new highs-new lows has been rising recently. While this isn’t enough by itself to guarantee a market rally, it’s at least a start in the right direction.
Source: WSJ
Before the market is ready to launch its next sustained rally, the number of Big Board-listed stocks making new lows needs to diminish below 40 for a few days to let us know that the immediate threat of internal selling pressure has ended. We should also see a reversal of the recent trend where more stocks make new lows than new highs on most days. Once we see the needed improvement in the new highs and lows, we’ll have confirmation that the internal condition of the broad market has sufficiently healed to allow the bulls to regain control of the short-term trend.
I’ve emphasized that an established bull market should be given every last benefit of the doubt before investors turn bearish. I further believe in letting the stock market confirm its reversal rather than trying to anticipate it. Experience teaches that trying to time a market bottom is a difficult and potentially frustrating endeavor. If the bears are correct in their assertions that the October decline began a bear market, however, we should already see evidence of it in the form of another free-fall in the major averages. For now, participants are urged to walk cautiously and refrain from initiating new long positions in stocks and ETFs. However, investors should also continue to assume the bull market remains intact as long as the corporate earnings growth trend remains up and the 10-year Treasury yield isn't spiking above 4%.
In the meantime, investors can maintain longer-term investment positions to the stock market via ETFs and outperforming individual stocks in strong sectors. This includes, in particular, the consumer staples sector, which has shown relative strength versus the S&P 500 Index in recent months. With earnings growth still on a positive trajectory, the probability is strong that the large cap major averages will trend higher in the coming six months.
Disclosure: I am/we are long XLP.
